21 minutes read

Environment doctor and compatibility matrix

Offing can inspect its execution environment without scanning source files:

offing doctor .
offing doctor . --json

The doctor checks the Node.js runtime, installed package entry points, local MCP server, portable Agent Skill, shared plugin prerequisites, and local or CI workspace. It is read-only: it does not change configuration, execute suggested repairs, start a network listener, or upload repository data.

offing doctor --system also asks node, python3, go, java, dotnet, and terraform for their version (--version, or -version for Java, which works on every release) and matches each against the bundled end-of-life and end-of-support rules. The report lists each tool, its release line, and its status in a system array; tools that are not installed are skipped. A tool that is out of support is a warning, not a failure. Nothing else is run and nothing uses the network.

Text and JSON are generated from the same deterministic result. The JSON contract is offing.doctor.v1; its schema is schemas/doctor.v1.schema.json. A failed check always includes a concrete remediation. Warnings describe usable but not yet stable integration paths and do not make the command fail.

Compatibility matrix

Matrix version: 2026-10-15 / v1

Surface Combination Status Notes

CLI Node.js 22+ on macOS Supported Same deterministic CLI and JSON contracts; the full check runs on macOS in CI.
CLI Node.js 24 on Linux Supported Part of the CI matrix next to Node.js 22.
CLI Node.js 22+ on Windows Supported The full check runs on Windows in CI on every pull request.
GitHub Actions Ubuntu runner Supported Composite Action, annotations, baselines, severity gate, and JSON artifact.
GitHub Actions macOS runner Experimental Expected to work through bash; not yet in the required runner matrix.
GitHub Actions Windows runner Unsupported The current composite Action requires bash. Use the CLI explicitly if available.
GitLab CI Linux runner using the CLI Experimental Doctor detects GITLAB_CI and CI_PROJECT_DIR; a Catalog component is not published yet.

Agent Skill Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or Gemini CLI Supported Project installation validated through the skills CLI on 2026-10-15.
Agent Skill Other hosts supporting the open Agent Skills directory format Experimental The portable files can be copied or linked, but these hosts are not in the representative install gate.

v1 compatibility guarantees

From 1.0.0, the 1.x line is a SemVer compatibility promise: a consumer that pins offing@^1 (or a specific 1.x release) can rely on the contracts below without a surprise break in a minor or patch release. Removals and replacements still follow the deprecation policy; this section states what each contract guarantees and how long that guarantee lasts on the 1.x line.

Scans stay offline and need no account. That property is part of the v1 promise and is not relaxed in a 1.x release.

Support windows on 1.x

Kind Window on the 1.x line
A versioned document (offing.*.vN), its JSON Schema file, the detector SDK API version, the registry format, or the data-bundle format Supported for the whole 1.x line. A successor (vN+1) may ship in a minor release; the older version keeps working at least through the versioned-format notice period and is not removed before 2.0.0.
CLI commands, flags, and environment variables marked stable in the docs Supported for the whole 1.x line. A rename or removal needs the unversioned notice period and lands no earlier than 2.0.0.
MCP tools, resources, prompts, and their documented input fields Same as CLI flags: whole 1.x line; removal only after notice, and not before 2.0.0.
GitHub Action and GitLab component inputs whose default preserves current behavior Same as CLI flags.
Exit-code classes (policy 1, usage 2, data 3, parse 4, internal 5) Stable for the whole 1.x line. New classes get new numbers; existing numbers are never renumbered.
Surfaces the matrix marks Supported or Beta Get the windows above.
Surfaces the matrix marks Experimental Usable, but may change in any minor release with a CHANGELOG entry; no multi-release window.
Node.js and other runtimes listed in the matrix Dropped from the matrix only after that runtime reaches its own end of life, and only with a deprecation note in the release before the drop.

A 1.x patch fixes behavior or security and does not add fields. A 1.x minor may add optional fields, commands, tools, or inputs. A required field, a rename, a type change, or a removal of a versioned format requires a new document version and the windows above — not a silent break inside 1.x.

Per-contract guarantees

Each row is a published contract. The guarantee is the machine-readable shape: identifiers, field names, types, and exit codes. Help text, warning prose, and field order may change in any release. Consumers must ignore fields they do not know.

Contract Identifier / schema Guarantee on 1.x
Scan result offing.scan.v1 · scan.v1.schema.json Required fields and types stay; optional fields may appear in a minor. A breaking change ships as offing.scan.v2 while v1 remains accepted for the window.
Dependency check offing.check.v1 · check.v1.schema.json Same additive rules. Status values already documented keep their meaning.
Migration context offing.context.v1 · context.v1.schema.json Packet shape stays; new optional sections may appear.
Deprecation list offing.deprecations.v1 · deprecations.v1.schema.json Compact list shape stays for agents and planners.
Verification offing.verification.v1 · verification.v1.schema.json Re-scan result shape stays.
Doctor offing.doctor.v1 · doctor.v1.schema.json Check and summary shape stays; new optional checks may appear.
Capabilities manifest offing.capabilities.v1 · capabilities.v1.schema.json Manifest shape stays; new optional capability or surface entries may appear.
Baseline offing.baseline.v1 · baseline.v1.schema.json File format stays so CI baselines written under 1.x keep loading.
Config offing.config.v1 · config.v1.schema.json Documented keys keep their meaning; new optional keys may appear.
Rule document ebb.rule.v1 · rule.v1.schema.json Rule view shape stays for MCP resources and tooling.
Fix plan offing.fix.v1 · fix.v1.schema.json Plan shape stays.
Data status ebb.data-status.v1 · data-status.v1.schema.json Status shape stays.
CLI errors offing.error.v1 error.code classes and exit codes stay as in Exit codes.
Detector SDK offing.detector.v1 · src/sdk.ts Detectors written to this API keep loading; a v2 API may ship in parallel.
Registry file ebb.registry.v2 · registry.v2.schema.json v2 registries keep validating and loading; a v3 may ship in parallel.
Data bundle ebb.data-bundle.v1 · data-bundle.v1.schema.json Bundle manifest shape stays; older bundles remain accepted for the window after a successor appears.
MCP server Tool names, resource URIs, and input fields in MCP Listed tools and resources keep working; new tools or optional inputs may appear. Output documents use the rows above.
GitHub Action / GitLab component Input names in GitHub Action and GitLab Documented inputs keep their meaning; new inputs default to current behavior.
SARIF export SARIF 2.1.0 from scan --format sarif Remains valid SARIF 2.1.0; field mapping changes that would break code scanning need notice as for versioned formats.
Agent Skill Portable skill layout and trigger description Install and discovery paths for Supported hosts stay; host-specific packaging marked Experimental follows the experimental window.

Outside the v1 promise

These change without a contract break and are not covered by the windows above:

  • Lifecycle findings and rules. Bundled data can add, change, or remove a finding when evidence changes. Pin a data version or use a baseline to stabilize CI.
  • Detector maturity moves. Promoting or demoting a detector between Experimental, Beta, and Supported follows decision 0013.
  • Bug fixes that correct a wrong location, match, or message.
  • Internals not exported from src/index.ts or named in a schema, including maintainer scripts and test fixtures.
  • Human-readable wording in CLI help, finding prose, and documentation.

Until 1.0.0 is tagged, Offing is still pre-1.0: the deprecation policy already applies, and this section is the contract that 1.0.0 will publish. Issue tracking for the release is in the v1 epic.

Deprecation policy

Offing reports other projects' deprecations. Its own interfaces follow the policy below, so a script, an agent, or a plugin built on Offing keeps working long enough to move.

What the policy covers

Interface Version identifier Additive change Breaking change
CLI commands, flags, and environment variables None A new command, flag, or variable. The old form is deprecated for a full window, then removed.
JSON output of scan, check, explain, context, doctor, and the other --json commands schemaVersion, for example offing.scan.v1 A new optional field, added in a minor release. Consumers must ignore fields they do not know. A new document version such as offing.scan.v2; v1 keeps working for the window.
JSON Schemas in schemas/ File name, for example scan.v1.schema.json A new optional property. A new *.v2.schema.json file; the v1 file stays for the window.
MCP tools, resources, and prompts Tool and resource URIs, input field names, and the same output schemaVersion A new tool, prompt, optional input, or optional output field. A new window, then a removal or a new output version.
Detector SDK (src/sdk.ts) offing.detector.v1 A new optional member or a new context field. offing.detector.v2; the engine keeps loading v1 detectors during the window.
Registry format ebb.registry.v2 A new optional rule or registry field, accepted by the validator in the same release. ebb.registry.v3; v2 registries are still read during the window.
Data bundle ebb.data-bundle.v1 A new optional manifest field. A new bundle version; the old one is still accepted during the window.
GitHub Action and GitLab component inputs Input names A new input whose default preserves current behavior. The old input or behavior is deprecated for a full window, then removed.

The contract is the machine-readable part: command names, exit codes, field names, types, and schema versions. Human-readable wording, help text, warning prose, and field order may change in any release. A new optional field may appear in a v1 document in a minor release; a required field, a rename, a removal, or a type change requires a new version. Patch releases fix behavior but do not add fields.

Notice periods

Change Minimum notice before removal
CLI flag, environment variable, Action or component input, MCP tool, prompt, resource, or input field 90 days and one minor release, whichever ends later.
A versioned format: JSON document, schema file, registry, bundle, or detector API 12 months and two minor releases after its successor ships.

The window starts in the release that announces the deprecation, not in the release that removes it, and it is measured from that release's date. Extensions are allowed; shortening a window is not, except for a security or correctness problem (below).

Before 1.0, semantic versioning would permit a minor release to break an interface; this policy is deliberately stricter and already applies. From 1.0.0, the v1 compatibility guarantees lock the same windows into the SemVer major line. Surfaces the matrix marks Experimental may change in any minor release with a CHANGELOG entry; Beta and Supported surfaces get the windows above. Runtime support is listed in the matrix; a runtime is dropped from it only after the runtime reaches its own end of life and with a deprecation note in the release before the drop.

Removal process

  1. Open an issue labeled deprecation that names the interface, the replacement, and the intended removal release.
  2. Record it in the table below with the release it was deprecated in and the earliest release or date it may be removed.
  3. Announce it in a release: a CHANGELOG entry, a note in the docs for the interface, and the replacement and migration step. Where the interface can warn at runtime, a CLI flag or environment variable prints one line to stderr; an MCP tool or input is marked deprecated in its description.
  4. Keep it working for the full window. Only fixes and security changes are made to a deprecated interface, and its behavior must not drift toward the replacement.
  5. Remove it in the first release after the window. The CHANGELOG entry says so, the docs stop describing it, and a versioned format's old file is retired together with runtime support for it. The issue is linked from the release notes.
  6. If the replacement is not ready, extend the window in the table and say why in the issue. A deprecation without a documented replacement is not opened.

A security vulnerability, data corruption, or a contract that would make a lifecycle answer unsafe to act on may be fixed or removed in the next patch release. The release notes name the change, and a vulnerability is reported through SECURITY.md.

What is not a deprecation

  • Lifecycle findings. Rules and their evidence are data, not an interface. A data update can add, change, or remove a finding at any time; a baseline or a pinned data version is how a project stabilizes its results. A new finding is not a breaking change.
  • Detector coverage and maturity. Moving a detector between Experimental, Beta, and Supported, or reading a new declaration form, changes what a scan reports. Decision 0013 governs those changes.
  • Bug fixes. Correcting a wrong location, rule match, or message is not a deprecation, even when the corrected output differs from the old one.
  • Internals. Modules that are not exported from src/index.ts or named in a schema, the tools/ maintainer scripts, test fixtures, and plugin packaging internals may change at any time.

Current deprecations

Interface Deprecated in May be removed after Replacement
None — — —

Ecosystem coverage

Detector ecosystem Status Coverage
CI runner images Supported pool.vmImage in azure-pipelines.yml is matched against reviewed Azure hosted-image rules. GitLab image and services values are unclassified. CircleCI orbs, dynamic values, and floating aliases are unclassified; other CircleCI images are not judged. See CI runner images.
Container base images Supported FROM lines in Dockerfiles and Containerfiles and services.*.image in Compose files, for Docker Hub official images with a vendor lifecycle. See Container base images.
.NET Supported global.json, project files, Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props, and packages.lock.json, for .NET release lines past end of support and deprecated NuGet packages. See .NET.
Go Supported go and toolchain directives in go.mod and go.work, and direct require entries, for Go release lines past end of support. See Go.
Java and Kotlin (JVM) Supported JDK declarations in pom.xml, Gradle build scripts, .java-version, .sdkmanrc, and .tool-versions, and direct Maven dependencies, for non-LTS JDK releases past end of support and moved artifacts. See Java and Kotlin.
Kubernetes APIs Supported The literal apiVersion and kind in YAML manifests, Helm chart templates, and kustomization patches, for API versions the Kubernetes project says are no longer served, and Chart.yaml dependencies that still point at the retired Helm stable or incubator repositories. See Kubernetes APIs.
GitHub Actions Supported Selected first-party Action lifecycle rules and exact workflow locations.
Node.js and npm Supported Runtime declarations, direct dependencies, lockfiles, and supported source usages.
PHP Supported Pinned runtime declarations in .php-version, .tool-versions, composer.json, and composer.lock, for PHP release lines past end of support and abandoned Composer packages. See PHP.
Python Supported Runtime declarations, direct dependencies, common lockfiles, and supported source usages.
Ruby Supported Pinned runtime declarations in .ruby-version, .tool-versions, the Gemfile ruby directive, and Gemfile.lock RUBY VERSION, plus direct gems, for Ruby release lines past end of support and yanked gems. Gem rules can list source usages in Ruby files.
Rust Supported The pinned toolchain in rust-toolchain(.toml) and direct dependencies in Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, for toolchains older than the newest stable release and unmaintained crates. See Rust.
Swift Supported .swift-version and .xcode-version pins, the swift-tools-version line and literal from: / exact: dependencies in Package.swift, and resolved pin versions in Package.resolved, for Xcode releases App Store Connect no longer accepts and Swift toolchain lines with a lifecycle rule. The iOS deployment target (IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET) of an application target in an .xcodeproj project.pbxproj, for iOS releases App Store Connect no longer accepts. Libraries and platforms: minimums in Package.swift are not read for it. See Swift.
Android Supported Literal compileSdk, minSdk, targetSdk, and buildToolsVersion in build.gradle and build.gradle.kts, Android Gradle Plugin and Kotlin Android plugin versions in settings.gradle(.kts), agp and kotlin keys in libs.versions.toml, and string-notation Maven dependencies, matched to reviewed rules. Bundled rules cover Google Play Billing Library majors 5 through 9. SDK and plugin declarations produce a finding only when a rule names them. See Android.
C and C++ Supported cmake_minimum_required, C and C++ language standards, and compiler version checks in CMakeLists.txt; direct requirements in conanfile.txt and conanfile.py; and direct dependencies and builtin-baseline in vcpkg.json. Bundled rules cover CMake policy versions older than 3.5 (removed) and from 3.5 up to 3.10 (deprecated). See C and C++.
Dart and Flutter Supported Resolved packages and SDK constraints in pubspec.lock, direct dependencies and environment constraints in pubspec.yaml, and the Flutter version pinned in .fvmrc and .fvm/fvm_config.json, for Dart SDK releases past end of support and discontinued pub packages. See Dart and Flutter.
Deno and Bun Supported Exact runtime pins in deno.json, deno.jsonc, bunfig.toml, .bun-version, and .tool-versions, for Deno and Bun release lines past end of life. Version ranges, floating aliases, and environment variables are not matched. See Deno and Bun.
Database runtimes Experimental Image tags of postgres, mysql, mariadb, redis, and mongo services in Compose files, and literal engine versions on AWS (engine and engine_version), Azure (version), and Google Cloud SQL (database_version) managed database resources in *.tf, for major and minor lines past end of life or standard support. Bundled rules cover PostgreSQL 11 through 13 and MySQL 5.7 and 8.0, Azure Database for PostgreSQL 11 through 13 and MySQL 5.7, and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL 9.6 through 13 and MySQL 5.6 and 5.7. Variables in Terraform version attributes are listed as unclassified. See Database runtimes.
Elixir and Mix Supported Pinned Elixir and Erlang/OTP versions in .tool-versions, the project elixir: constraint and direct Hex deps in mix.exs, and resolved Hex packages in mix.lock, for Elixir and OTP release lines past end of support and retired Hex packages. See Elixir and Mix.
Scala and sbt Supported Pinned Scala versions in .scala-version and literal scalaVersion settings in build.sbt, and sbt.version in project/build.properties, for Scala 2.11, frozen Scala 3.0–3.2 lines, and sbt 0.13. See Scala and sbt.
Shell and PowerShell Supported Literal #Requires -Version directives in *.ps1 and *.psm1, PowerShellVersion in *.psd1 manifests, and pinned mcr.microsoft.com/powershell image tags in .github/workflows files, for PowerShell releases past end of support. Bundled rules cover PowerShell 6.x and 7.0 through 7.3. Shell names such as shell: pwsh and Bash images carry no version and are not matched. See Shell and PowerShell.
Terraform Experimental required_version and required_providers constraints in *.tf, locked provider versions in .terraform.lock.hcl, the Terraform CLI version pinned in .terraform-version and .tool-versions, and managed Kubernetes control-plane versions in *.tf for Amazon EKS, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Azure Kubernetes Service, for Terraform CLI and Kubernetes release lines past end of support. Bundled rules cover CLI lines 1.10 through 1.14 and EKS, GKE, and AKS versions 1.33 and earlier; provider rules are not bundled yet. See Terraform.
Serverless runtimes Supported Runtime on AWS SAM and CloudFormation functions and Globals, provider.runtime and per-function runtime in serverless.yml, and Terraform runtime on aws_lambda_function plus Google Cloud Functions runtimes and Azure function-app application_stack version pins. Bundled rules cover selected AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions identifiers that the vendors list as end-of-life. See Serverless runtimes.
Other language and platform ecosystems Unsupported Report the limitation; do not infer lifecycle status without a detector.

Supported means the combination is part of the documented product contract. Experimental means it is usable but lacks a complete release gate or stable distribution package. For detectors, Experimental, Beta, and Supported have the meanings and the evidence requirements in decision 0013, and the level of each is recorded in benchmarks/thresholds.json. Unsupported means Offing does not currently claim the combination works.

Swift detector

The swift detector is supported: its level is recorded as stable in benchmarks/thresholds.json, and the precision floor is enforced. Eighty-five public repositories in Validation cover it. Supported forms, limits, and data sources are documented in Swift. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/swift.json and ship in the data bundle.

Dart and Flutter detector

The dart detector is supported: its level is recorded as stable in benchmarks/thresholds.json, and the precision floor is enforced. Seventy-five public repositories are pinned for it in benchmarks/public-repositories/. Supported files, declaration forms, matching rules, and limits are documented in Dart and Flutter. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/dart.json and ship in the data bundle.

Elixir and Mix detector

The elixir detector is supported: its level is recorded as stable in benchmarks/thresholds.json. Supported files, declaration forms, matching rules, and limits are documented in Elixir and Mix. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/elixir.json and ship with the package (see Lifecycle data).

Scala and sbt detector

The scala detector is stable: its level is recorded as stable in benchmarks/thresholds.json, and the precision floor is enforced. Eighty public repositories in Validation cover it (blind-selected by the 2026-11-07 rule). Supported files, declaration forms, matching rules, and limits are documented in Scala and sbt. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/scala.json and ship with the package (see Lifecycle data).

Database runtimes detector

The database detector is experimental: its level is recorded as experimental in benchmarks/thresholds.json. Five public repositories are pinned in benchmarks/public-repositories/: four targeted cases and one blind, zero-finding repository, with ground truth from the vendors' lifecycle sources. Supported files, declaration forms, matching rules, and limits are documented in Database runtimes. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/database.json and ship in the data bundle.

Shell and PowerShell detector

The shell detector is supported: its level is recorded as stable in benchmarks/thresholds.json. Forty-three public repositories are pinned under the shell ecosystem, thirty-nine of them chosen blind, with nine zero-finding controls. Each expected finding was checked by reading its line at the pinned commit against Microsoft's PowerShell support lifecycle, independently of Offing output. Supported files, declaration forms, matching rules, and limits are documented in Shell and PowerShell. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/shell.json and ship in the data bundle.

Terraform detector

The terraform detector is experimental: its level is recorded as experimental in benchmarks/thresholds.json. Supported files, declaration forms, matching rules, and limits are documented in Terraform. Its lifecycle rules are in registry/terraform.json and ship in the data bundle.

Monorepos

The npm and Python detectors read every package of a workspace, not only the repository root. Packages are found from the declarations the package managers use: workspaces in package.json (npm and Yarn, array or packages form), pnpm-workspace.yaml (with ! exclusions), lerna.json, and [tool.uv.workspace] members and exclude in pyproject.toml. Globs support *, ?, and **.

  • Findings name the package's own file, for example packages/a/package.json, and carry the usages inside that package's directory; usages outside every package stay with the root.
  • A workspace without its own lockfile resolves versions against the root's lockfile.
  • Discovery is bounded: eight directory levels, 500 packages, symbolic links never followed, and node_modules, vendor, dist, build, target, virtual environments, and fixture directories skipped.
  • A malformed workspace manifest is skipped, so one bad package does not hide the others. A malformed root package.json is still an error.
  • Without a workspace declaration only the root is scanned, as before. Python projects that are not uv workspaces (for example separate pyproject.toml files under services/) are not discovered.

CI behavior

  • In GitHub Actions, the doctor requires GITHUB_WORKSPACE to name an accessible checkout directory.
  • In GitLab CI, the doctor requires CI_PROJECT_DIR to name an accessible checkout directory.
  • Outside those environments, it reports local execution and does not require CI variables.

The checks only read Offing's own packaged metadata and test workspace accessibility. They do not inspect secrets, tokens, repository contents, or remote services.
